name: libzmq (ZeroMQ)
workload: PUB/SUB payload throughput (MB/s, 'Payload Throughput' column) of the bml-pub-sub harness: 5000 messages per run, payloads 1 KB to 512 KB, inproc, ipc and tcp transports on one host, 1/2/4/8 subscribers, publisher interval 0 (send as fast as possible); one result row per configuration in results/results.csv.
claimed_speedup: No claim by the libzmq project; independent data. ZeroMQ had the highest payload throughput in 95 of 120 interval-0 configurations (inproc 26/40, ipc 34/40, tcp 35/40; nanomsg won the other 25, NNG none) (derived from page data). Geometric-mean ratio over NNG: 1.31x (tcp), 1.37x (ipc), 2.39x (inproc) at payloads 256-512 KB, and 1.34-1.57x at payloads up to 64 KB; over nanomsg: 1.51x (tcp), 1.59x (ipc), 3.03x (inproc) at 256-512 KB but only 1.05-1.13x at payloads up to 64 KB (derived from page data). Example row, one subscriber, tcp, 512 KB payload: ZeroMQ 2930 MB/s vs NNG 2018 MB/s vs nanomsg 1231 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Harness (bml/Makefile): gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2. libzmq and libnanomsg come from distro packages (apt libzmq3-dev, libnanomsg-dev; versions and build flags not stated in the repo). NNG v1.9.0 is built from source by install_bml.sh with plain 'cmake -G Ninja ..' and no build type given (whether that yields an optimised library was not verified).
tradeoffs: Message-oriented brokerless messaging library with a C API (core in C++98/C++11); sockets are not thread-safe, so callers must serialise access or use one socket per thread. The same suite's authors (per the search-result summary of the paper, which could not be opened) report nanomsg ahead on small-message latency, CPU use and memory, so the throughput lead is not a lead on every metric.
caveats: Numbers are derived by me from the paper's published dataset results/results.csv in hitachienergy/messaging-libraries-benchmark (a fork, commrade-goad/nng-rtt-lite-benchmark, carries an identical file); the paper itself (arXiv 2508.07934, Hitachi Energy Research) was EGRESS_BLOCKED and not opened, so hardware (CPU model) and library versions are not confirmed here. Tier B, not A, because CPU model and distro-package build flags are missing. The benchmark is one row per configuration (the runner script uses --runs 4, presumably averaged), a single host over loopback. At payloads up to 64 KB all three libraries post near-identical MB/s (e.g. at 1 KB with one subscriber ZeroMQ 18.0, nanomsg 16.9-18.1 and NNG 16.5-17.5 MB/s across the three transports), which suggests the harness is publisher-paced there, so the 1.05-1.13x lead over nanomsg at small payloads is not meaningful. nanomsg won 25 of the 120 configurations (mostly inproc, 14 of them). libzmq's own repo (perf/ directory: local_lat, remote_thr, inproc_thr and similar) ships measurement tools and no published results, and zeromq.org was blocked, so the project makes no checkable comparison itself. The awesome-list licence tag (GPL-3.0-or-later) is out of date: the repo page shows MPL-2.0.

name: Mongoose
baseline: lwIP (STM32 Cube configuration, raw API) TCP/IP stack
workload: Vendor comparison on an ST Nucleo-F746ZG board of Mongoose's built-in TCP/IP stack and HTTP server against lwIP: HTTP requests per second, firmware (flash) size and RAM.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (pages EGRESS_BLOCKED). Search-result summary of the mongoose.ws lwIP-vs-Mongoose article: on a Nucleo-F746ZG Mongoose reached 1080 requests/s against 286 requests/s for lwIP raw (about 3.8x, derived from the snippet) with 28k vs 114k firmware size. A second search-result summary of the integration-benchmark article lists flash 50,140 vs 67,020 bytes and RAM 22,524 vs 31,504 bytes (Mongoose vs lwIP), and 3 files / 32k lines vs 279 files / 105k lines to integrate.
hardware: ST Nucleo-F746ZG (STM32F746, Cortex-M7) per search snippet
tradeoffs: Dual licensed: GPLv2 or a paid commercial licence (Cesanta), so closed-source products need the commercial licence. Two-file amalgamation (mongoose.c, mongoose.h) with its own TCP/IP stack for bare metal and RTOS, or it can run on top of lwIP; it is a full networking and web library, not only a TCP/IP stack, so the lwIP comparison is partly of different scope.
caveats: First-party vendor measurement by the company selling Mongoose (and its commercial licence). mongoose.ws is EGRESS_BLOCKED from this environment, so the article was not opened; every figure here comes from WebSearch result summaries, which are machine-written, and the two summaries differ in which numbers they quote (1080/286 requests/s and 28k/114k appear in one only, the byte counts in the other, and the source article for the 1080/286 figures may be mongoose.ws/articles/lwip-vs-mongoose Part 1 rather than the URL given). Compiler, flags, lwIP configuration (raw API, sockets or netconn) and the request workload were not seen. The only reachable GitHub page, the repo README, links the article ('lwIP vs Mongoose - TCP/IP Stack Integration Benchmark') and holds no numbers; the repo has no benchmark directory. The size figures are footprint, not speed.
